articles.title_zh: Dow falls 400 points as 10-year yield rises to highest level in 24 years: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Inflation fears intensified in September, pushing the near-term outlook in the New York Federal Reserve's monthly survey to its highest level in nearly 3½ years.
The central bank's Survey of Consumer Expectations indicated that the median view for inflation over the next 12 months rose to 3.9%, up 0.3 percentage point from August and the highest level since May 2023, when the figure was at 4.1%.
Similarly, the survey found that household spending growth is expected to hit 5.5%, also up 0.3 percentage point month over month and the highest since May 2023.
The results come with Fed officials grappling over the proper setting of monetary policy as inflation holds well above the central bank's 2% target.
Markets largely expect the Federal Open Market Committee to keep benchmark rates steady when it meets later in October. Inflation in August came in lower than expected , according to the Fed's preferred gauge. In recent days several key officials, including New York Fed President John Williams, have said policymakers can afford to take their time when evaluating where interest rates should be set.
The survey did find that the outlook is better-anchored further out on the timeline. The three-year expectation edged up 0.1 percentage point to 3.3%, while the five-year view was unchanged at 3%.
Market-based indicators, though, are less positive.
One closely watched bond market indicator known as a breakeven shows the five-year outlook around its highest level of the year at 2.35%. Treasury yields have been soaring in recent weeks, hitting levels not seen since the early part of the century.
Fed officials consider expectations a key driver for inflation.
Surging energy costs are at the core of the inflation problem. Gasoline prices rose nearly 4% in August alone, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, while fuel oil surged more than 10%.
At the consumer level, utilities have filed for $23.1 billion in increases so far in 2026, according to PoweLines, a nonpartisan consumer advocacy group. The third quarter alone saw requests for $4.5 billion, the largest sum for the period on record. The New York Fed survey found consumers expect gas prices to rise by 4.8% over the next year, an increase of 0.2 percentage point from August.
While looking for the Fed to stay put at its next meeting, markets are pricing in a much more aggressive central bank in the years ahead. Fed funds futures contracts are implying a rate of 5.58% in five years. The current funds rate is targeted between 3.75%-4%.

articles.title_zh: Christa Pike Live Updates: Judge to Hear From Her Lawyers After Failed Execution
articles.content_orig:
• Happening now: A hearing is underway as attorneys for Christa Pike, the Tennessee inmate who survived an execution attempt , seek a court order to ensure the preservation of evidence in her botched execution .
• Pike’s condition: Pike is conscious and speaking one week after the failed execution, the attorneys say. After surviving two ostensibly lethal doses of pentobarbital, she was transferred to a hospital and received lifesaving medical care.
• What to know: Pike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, was to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years.
Attorneys for Christa Pike are asking Judge I’Ashea Myles for “continuous liberal access” to her, noting Pike currently has no way to contact her attorneys.
“TDOC (the Tennessee Department of Correction) continues to put up roadblocks, for not only the providers at the hospital, but for counsel, and so we would ask for an order granting continuous liberal access to Ms. Pike,” attorney Luke Ihnen said.
Before her attempted execution, Ihnen told Judge Myles, Pike had access to a tablet with which she could contact friends, family and attorneys.
Ihnen also requested that TDOC notify them before Pike is transferred from the hospital she is currently at and that she no longer he shackled to her hospital bed.
“Based on our understanding, medical staff have asked that the shackles be removed and have been denied that request by TDOC,” the attorney said.
Judge I’Ashea Myles pressed the state attorney on the emergency circumstances of today’s hearing as he argued the petitioners in the case have not requested discovery.
“We are here improvidently at this point in time,” Myles said. “And so, is it really fair to say to the petitioner, ‘Well, you haven’t moved on your underlying action’ when the petitioner was focused on what – I don’t want to put words in her mouth – but there was something that was more pressing than discovery in an underlying case.”
Myles continued, “So, can you really stand before the court and say, ‘Well, the petitioner hasn’t asked for any discovery’?”
The state’s attorney responded, “The state’s position is, as stated in our briefing, that discovery is governed by the rules of civil procedure, and those rules must be followed.”
Christa Pike regained consciousness yesterday, her attorney Luke Ihnen said in court, and has been unable to communicate with her legal team since her botched execution.
“Part of the issue that we are facing is up until yesterday, our client was unconscious, unable to communicate with counsel, unable to communicate with her medical providers, and without her consent, we are not able to to bring a new lawsuit,” Ihnen said.
“And so, Ms. Pike, as it’s been widely reported, regained consciousness yesterday and is speaking limitedly, and so you know obviously I think the original complaint stands, but you know we are not – we have not been authorized by our client to pursue a new cause of action.”
In January, Pike’s lawyers filed a complaint in the Davidson County Chancery Court challenging execution methods. That complaint was transferred to the state’s Supreme Court, where it was dismissed over procedural issues.
Ihnen said Pike’s lawyers haven’t been able to discuss with her the possibility of refiling a similar complaint or other possible legal next steps.
Today’s hearing is specifically over a narrow emergency motion from Pike’s legal team to preserve state records related to her execution.
The Davidson County Chancery Court, after hearing arguments, decided it retained jurisdiction in the procedural posture of the case after Christa Pike’s botched execution attempt.
Pike’s attorneys argued that the court should take up the case, saying the case has drawn notable “because of the extraordinary circumstances surrounding that motion for preservation of evidence .”
Remember: Pike’s lawyers filed an emergency motion Friday to ensure the preservation of evidence, alleging the Tennessee Department of Correction (TDOC) inflicted “a cruel and unusual punishment” on Pike “through its deliberate indifference to her basic medical needs and reckless disregard of basic medical practices and their own lethal injection protocol.”
The state has asked the court to deny an emergency motion, arguing (TDOC) “is already bound to preserve the targeted evidence under a federal district court’s longstanding preservation order.”
Judge I’Ashea Myles began the hearing by calling Luke Ihnen, one of Christa Pike’s attorneys, to the lectern. All eyes in the courtroom are on Ihnen as he speaks with the judge about procedural issues in the case.
Dozens of media members are in the courtroom gallery, typing as the attorney speaks. The judge is looking back and forth between her computer and Ihnen.
The hearing is underway as attorneys for Christa Pike, the Tennessee inmate who survived an execution attempt, ask the court to preserve evidence related to her botched execution. The courtroom gallery is full with members of the press.
Pike is conscious and speaking one week after surviving two ostensibly lethal doses of pentobarbital, her attorneys said.
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer and was set to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years.
During the execution procedure on Christa Pike, executioners struggled to place IV lines, causing the pentobarbital to flow into her body rather than her bloodstream , according to Pike’s attorneys.
Those administering the lethal injection attempted to gain IV access to Pike using “at least seven needles,” an emergency motion to ensure the preservation of evidence, filed Friday, says. “One needle was bent in a 90-degree angle when it was removed.”
Randy Spivey, one of Pike’s lawyers, told reporters she was cooperating with the execution team and even communicating where they should try to insert the IV lines.
Pike’s attorneys had previously warned the state of her history of difficulties with finding vein access. The execution team spent an hour trying to establish an IV line.
When Pike arrived at the Nashville-area hospital following the botched execution, her attorneys said in the motion, her arms were “swollen, burned, and blistered.” Pentobarbital “burns upon contact, including skin, tissue, and veins,” they said.
Attorneys for Christa Pike will hold a news conference after today’s hearing, where they plan to seek a court order to preserve evidence related to what they describe as her botched execution .
Attorneys Luke Ihnen of Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee and Randy Spivey of the Tennessee Office of the Post-Conviction Defender are expected to provide an update on Pike’s condition.
Tennessee’s lethal injection execution protocol, which the Tennessee Department of Correction said it acted according to throughout Christa Pike’s failed execution , is laid out in a 44-page document created by the Department of Correction, according to a copy obtained by the Death Penalty Information Center.
The step-by-step protocol is used to “ensure the humane and constitutional execution of inmates sentenced to death” and prohibits officials from straying from the procedure.
“There will be no deviation from the Protocol except by order of the Commissioner,” the protocol states.
The protocol approves only a one-drug method of lethal injection, specifically pentobarbital, a barbiturate that can cause death. The protocol states 100 ml of a 50 mg/ml solution of pentobarbital (a total of 5 grams) shall be checked to verify its contents and expiration dates 30 days before a scheduled execution.
The document lays out procedures leading up to, during and after the execution. Personnel prepare the primary 100 ml dose of pentobarbital solution in syringes, as well as a backup set “if the inmate is not deceased,” the protocol states.
There is no protocol for what happens if that second set does not work.

articles.title_zh: Webull stock on track for worst day in a year after lawmakers flag ties to China

Oops, something went wrong
Webull ( BULL ) stock plunged 20% on Wednesday after US lawmakers reportedly flagged that the company is "tied in structural ways" to China's government, risking its regulatory standing in the US.
The stock was on track for its worst daily drop since April 17, 2025, according to Dow Jones and FactSet market data. Over the past month, the stock has cratered by 40%.
On Wednesday, CNBC reported that a bipartisan House Select Committee on China assessment found that the company poses a national security risk and that concerns about its operations have "escalated" over the past year.
Webull is a digital investment platform headquartered in St. Petersburg, Fla. Yet the congressional report stated there was "a profound gap" between how the company marketed itself as a US company and how it is actually controlled.
"Webull's ownership architecture, technical workforce, technology infrastructure, cross-border data routing, corporate financing, and compliance frameworks are tied in structural ways to the People's Republic of China," the report said, per CNBC.
The company was founded in 2016 by former Alibaba ( BABA ) employee Anquan Wang and was affiliated with the Chinese holding company Hunan Fumi Information Technology. It went public on the Nasdaq via a special-purpose acquisition merger with SK Growth Opportunities in 2025.
Webull has 28.2 million users, and roughly 85% of its funded accounts are held by US users, according to SEC filings. The committee raised concerns that Webull's US customer data could be exposed should Webull be compelled to comply with Chinese laws and government requests.
Webull pushed back on the report, telling CNBC that it contained "significant inaccuracies and unsupported conclusions."

articles.title_orig: Suit Seeks $549 Million for Historically Black College, Citing Disparities
articles.title_zh: Suit Seeks $549 Million for Historically Black College, Citing Disparities
articles.content_orig:
A group of current and former Lincoln University students has filed a lawsuit against the State of Missouri.
The lawsuit claims that the school has been underfunded compared to the University of Missouri.
The State of Missouri, Gov. Mike Kehoe, the Coordinating Board of Higher Education of the State of Missouri, Department of Higher Education & Workforce Development Commissioner Dr. Bennett Boggs, and MU Chancellor Mun Choi were listed as defendants.
According to documents filed in the Western District of Missouri U.S. District Court, the lawsuit seeks “Equal Protection and Title VI claims alleging Missouri’s underfunding of Lincoln University and its performance-criteria funding formula perpetuate the vestiges of de jure segregated higher education; seeks declaratory and injunctive relief and Title VI damages.”
The Missouri Legislative Black Caucus issued a statement supporting Lincoln University.
“Lincoln University has served Missourians for generations, and its future matters to communities across our state,” said State Representative Michael Johnson, Chair of the Missouri Legislative Black Caucus.
“Lincoln University educates Missourians from every county, background, and political party,” Representative Johnson said.  “The Caucus is committed to working with colleagues across the aisle and with state leaders to support Lincoln’s continued success and to advance a fair, dependable approach to its funding.”
Lincoln University, a historically Black university, was founded in 1866 by soldiers from the 62nd and 65th United States Colored Infantries.

articles.title_orig: France halts use of stun grenades after boy's hand blown off in student protests
articles.title_zh: France halts use of stun grenades after boy's hand blown off in student protests
articles.content_orig:
France has suspended the use of stun grenades for policing student protests that have swept the country, after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off earlier this week.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said he had requested the pause until the facts of Monday's incident in Lens had been "clarified", with conflicting accounts offered by protesters and officials.
Several groups have complained of police using disproportionate force towards teenagers.
The disruption continued early on Wednesday with more than 500 schools fully or partially shut, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is due to speak about the school protests in an evening address.
Education Minister Édouard Geffray said 24 schools had been "set alight or vandalised" to such an extent that they would be shut for several weeks, affecting 30,000 pupils.
Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets on Tuesday to call for better school conditions and in some cities tear gas and water cannon were deployed. The interior ministry said 488 people were arrested and 43 members of the security forces were hurt.
Nuñez told French radio RTL that police watchdog IGPN had opened 18 investigations to determine whether officers had been "proportionate" during the demonstrations, which have spread from high school pupils to their parents, university students and unions.
"There is a police action that raises questions for all of us within the Ministry of the Interior; it's what happened in Lens," he said as he confirmed the suspension of stun grenades - weapons which are considered non-lethal and send out small rubber pellets when they detonate.
The 15-year-old boy's hand was torn off after a so-called anti-encirclement grenade was fired in unclear circumstances near the Auguste Béhal high school in the northern city near Lille.
Authorities have said he picked up the grenade which then exploded, but students have alleged he was hit directly after an officer fired. According to the local prefect, police had been confronted by more than 200 students throwing stones and fireworks.
The national secretary of policing union UNSA said he was sceptical about the move, saying it had been based "on emotion".
"We are dealing with increasingly violent people," Jean-Paul Nascimento told FranceInfo, cautioning that without the weapon to disperse crowds there may be more clashes at close quarters. "That's where there will perhaps be even more injuries," he warned.
Concerns have also been stoked by the case of a 14-year-old hit in the face with a tear gas grenade last week. The boy's lawyer said he had lost several teeth and suffered a fractured jaw in the incident at Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône, north-west of Paris, and a police officer has been charged.
And in a separate development on Wednesday, a 16-year-old suffered a serious hand injury outside a school in Strasbourg, reportedly while handling a mortar firework.
Prosecutors also said an investigation for attempted murder had been opened after a 17-year-old student protester complained an officer "held his head underwater" while trying to arrest him near a river in the north-eastern city of Belfort. French reports say the boy has himself been charged with aggravated assault for allegedly attacking the officer.
Addressing France's National Assembly on Wednesday, both Nuñez and Education Minister Geffray said the speed at which the protests had turned violent was unprecedented.
Geffray said dozens of headteachers and deputies had been injured, many deliberately so, and alleged the movement had been "very quickly infiltrated by ultra-violent groups".
"We have never seen anything like this," he said of the disorder which officials report has harmed more than 200 students and 700 police officers, and prompted more than 6,600 arrests.
Nuñez later said he found it "excessive to speak of police repression of the movement", insisting that officers were only acting in response to violence and damage.
The national coordinator of the radical-left France Unbowed (LFI) party said that it had taken "several children being maimed for life for Nuñez to give up using grenades against high school students".
The prime minister has accused LFI of trying to "sow chaos" during the protests ahead of elections to select President Emmanuel Macron's successor in April.
Its leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon is currently second in the opinion polls behind Marine Le Pen of the hard-right National Rally - who on Wednesday said Macron was "always on the side of attacking the police".
The president held an emergency meeting late on Tuesday with Prime Minister Lecornu and other key ministers to find a way out of the crisis after almost a quarter of all lycées were disrupted by the day's protests - with government figures putting the number of protesters at more than 250,000.
Lecornu announced that schools should set aside half the day for students to voice their concerns, and noted on social media that an online consultation seeking their opinions had drawn 30,000 responses within a day.
But students' unions - who put the number of protesters at 450,000 - maintain a fourth round of demonstrations is planned for Thursday in Paris and other cities, and told reporters they had requested a meeting with Lecornu due to a lack of "concrete measures" outlined so far.
The union representing school leaders told FranceInfo that a solution would require "something more than simple consultation periods", while the head of the USL high school union, Ryad Rani, told French radio on Wednesday: "We are telling M. Nuñez, calm your police officers down and call for restraint."

articles.title_zh: Was the Human Gut Healthier in Ancient Times?
articles.content_orig:

The gut microbiome is crucial for health and is affected strongly by lifestyle 1 . Many microorganisms commonly found in non-industrialized populations are disappearing or have become extinct in industrialized populations 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 . Studying which microorganisms have been long-term residents of the human gut and may have co-evolved with humans 2 , 7 , 8 could provide insights into how microbial biodiversity loss affects human health. However, the genetic complexities of microbial evolution and the plasticity of gut microbiome composition have made it challenging to resolve the evolutionary history of these long-term associations. Here we performed deep metagenomic sequencing of the Tsimane horticulturalists of Bolivia and compared their gut microbiomes with those of the Hadza hunter-gatherers of Tanzania 3 . These two populations, whose ancestors have been separated for tens of thousands of years, share 1,231 microbial species, most of which are rare in or absent from industrialized populations. Population genetic analyses of 636 of the shared species revealed patterns of microbial divergence and gene flow consistent with prehistoric human co-migration, with estimated split times that approximately align with human migration out of Africa and into the Americas. Our findings indicate that a diverse gut microbiome co-migrated with humans worldwide and has persisted over millennia. However, many of these species are now vanishing from industrialized populations and the consequences for human health remain uncertain.
Commensal gut bacteria play a complex part in human biology 1 , but the evolutionary history of these microbial relationships remains poorly characterized 9 . Identifying long-term associations between humans and microorganisms is important for understanding their co-evolution 7 , 10 , 11 , and this could reveal microbial species and functions integral to human health and physiology.
Direct observations of historical microbial relationships have been obtained by sequencing palaeofaeces 12 . This study suggested that ancient gut microbiomes were more similar to those of contemporary non-industrialized populations than to those of industrialized ones (the term industrialized here refers to post-industrial populations as well as those in advanced and ongoing stages of industrialization). However, the comparatively recent ages of existing palaeofaeces (around 1,000–2,000 years old), combined with the challenges of analysing degraded ancient DNA, makes it difficult to determine whether these microbial lineages have been faithfully transmitted over long evolutionary timescales (of around 10,000–100,000 years) or were acquired or transmitted more recently.
Comparative genomics methods provide an alternative approach to inferring evolutionary history from the patterns of genetic diversity among contemporary microbial genomes 8 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 . Building on previous work in non-human primates 2 , 8 , 19 , 20 , 21 , advances in strain-resolved metagenomics have made it possible to use this approach on gut microbial species sampled from human populations worldwide. Previous work has identified phylogenetic correlations between gut microbial genomes and their human populations of origin 7 , potentially consistent with long-term associations 18 , 22 , 23 . However, interpreting these correlations remains challenging because they require genome comparisons at the subspecies, or strain, level. Conventional phylogenetic methods 24 often fail in such settings because intra-species gene transfer and homologous recombination between strains produce mosaic patterns of ancestry that cannot be represented by a single phylogenetic tree 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 . These high rates of recombination make it difficult to distinguish ancient co-migration from other sources of population structure, such as geography or host lifestyle variation 22 , 23 . Moreover, existing strain-level analyses have been biased towards gut microbial species in industrialized populations 29 . These sampling biases have hindered our ability to infer the evolutionary history of the microbial taxa that are the most likely candidates for ancestral co-migration.
To address these challenges, we conducted deep metagenomic sequencing on faecal samples from the Tsimane horticulturalists of Bolivia (previously characterized using 16S ribosomal RNA sequencing 6 ) and compared their microbiomes with those of the Hadza hunter-gatherers of Tanzania 3 . These two cohorts represent unique and geographically distant contemporary populations whose ancestors separated thousands of years ago, providing a rare opportunity for examining human–microorganism co-migration patterns across a wide range of candidate ancestral microbial taxa. We identified more than 1,200 microbial species shared between the two populations, most of which (60%) were rare in or absent from industrialized populations. Using population genetic analyses that explicitly account for microbial recombination, we provide evidence of strain-level reproductive isolation that is stronger than that observed in microorganisms from comparable industrialized populations. These findings suggest the transgenerational maintenance of gut microbial communities throughout ancient human migrations, providing insights into the roles of horizontal gene transfer and host–microorganism co-evolution in the long-term structuring of the human microbiome.
The Tsimane people are Indigenous forager-horticulturalists living in the Bolivian Amazon. The individuals in this cohort live in six villages along the Maniqui River and three villages in a nearby forest region 6 . We performed deep metagenomic sequencing on 133 faecal samples collected from 85 Tsimane adults in 2009 and 2012–2013 (median depth = 31.9 gigabases; Extended Data Fig. 1a ). We recovered 12,746 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) representing 1,408 bacterial and archaeal species (Fig. 1a , Methods and Supplementary Table 1 ). We then compared these genomes with an analogous collection of 32,034 MAGs previously obtained from deeply sequenced microbiome samples of 137 Hadza hunter-gatherers in Tanzania 3 (Extended Data Fig. 1b ) to quantify how the gut microbial species of these populations have diverged over the past 100,000 years.

articles.title_orig: Three years after Oct. 7, Israeli strikes in Gaza grind on and deaths climb
articles.title_zh: Three years after Oct. 7, Israeli strikes in Gaza grind on and deaths climb
articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu lays a wreath during a state memorial ceremony in memory of those killed in the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel, at Mount Herzl cemetery in Jerusalem on Oct. 5. Debbie Hill/Pool UPI via AP hide caption
TEL AVIV, Israel — As Israel marks three years since Hamas launched its surprise Oct. 7 attacks, Israelis are reeling from new revelations in Israeli and U.S. media that the country had been repeatedly warned by its regional allies that Hamas was planning to attack.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was personally warned about a potential Hamas attack, and his security agencies were notified repeatedly, in the weeks and days leading up to Oct. 7, 2023, four people in the Middle East with direct knowledge of the warnings told NPR.
The Israeli newspaper Haaretz , The New York Times and The Atlantic first reported about the warnings.
Netanyahu has denied he was warned, calling the reports "fake news" and filing a defamation lawsuit last week against Israeli news outlets that published them. He and his defense minister have issued new warnings that Hamas could try to attack or "challenge" Israel on this Oct. 7 memorial day and leading up to national elections later this month.
But the Oct. 7, 2023, security failure — as well as Netanyahu's repeated refusal to take responsibility for it — has become a lightning rod in Israel as the prime minister seeks a new term in national elections this month.
"You didn't protect my son," yelled out one bereaved Israeli father whose son was killed in the Hamas-led attack, as the prime minister spoke at a memorial ceremony this week for the victims.
One warning came directly from the leader of Hamas in Gaza weeks before Oct. 7, a Palestinian mediator told NPR and other media outlets.
Former Palestinian Authority official Sufian Abu Zaida said he helped mediate secret Hamas-Israel talks for more than a year leading up to Oct. 7. He said Hamas wanted Israel to release Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and offered in exchange to release two living Israeli hostages and the bodies of two Israeli soldiers held in Gaza for years. But he said Israel was unwilling to release as many prisoners as Hamas had demanded.
On Sept. 14, 2023, Abu Zaida said, Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar dictated a message for him to deliver to Israel: "By the end of September, we will put cards on the table. There will be an earthquake in the negotiations, and the Israelis should prepare to empty their prisons."
He did not know what kind of earthquake Sinwar meant, but he said he sent the message to an Israeli intelligence official who acknowledged receiving it and to Mohammed Dahlan, a Palestinian confidant of the leader of the United Arab Emirates.
"What happened [on] the 7th of October is needless," Abu Zaida told NPR.
Days before the Oct. 7 attacks, the leader of the United Arab Emirates, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, called Netanyahu and told him that Hamas' leader in Gaza was planning a big assault against Israel, according to a person close to Dahlan. Dahlan was the Palestinian Authority's head of security in Gaza before Hamas seized control of the territory in 2007.
The Emirati leader told Netanyahu in a phone call that lasted more than 40 minutes that a "quake" would hit the region if no progress was achieved regarding a prisoner deal between Hamas and Israel, the person said.
The person spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity because of the diplomatic sensitivity of the call. The phone call was previously reported by Haaretz and The New York Times .
The UAE did not deny the report, saying only that it maintained dialogue with Israel.
People visit a memorial at a police station attacked by Hamas on Oct. 7, 2023, three years prior, in Sderot, southern Israel, on Oct. 4. Oded Balilty/AP hide caption
A senior Egyptian official told NPR that Egypt had specific intelligence about Hamas movements and that Egypt's head of intelligence at the time, Abbas Kamel, had traveled to Israel with two other senior officials and met with Israel's Mossad and Shin Bet intelligence chiefs.
The official said Kamel relayed a warning that Gaza was on the verge of an "explosion" because of Israel's blockade, the condition of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and concerns that Israel might move to annex the occupied West Bank.
The official was not authorized to speak publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity. The Atlantic reported that Kamel's visit to Israel was on Sept 26.
Nimrod Novik, a fellow at the Israel Policy Forum think tank and a former top adviser to late Israeli Prime Minister Shimon Peres, told NPR that he was informed before Oct. 7 by a person with firsthand knowledge that Egypt had delivered warnings to several senior Israeli officials that "Gaza is about to explode in your face."
Novik said one warning was an "urgent and dramatic message" from Egypt, delivered to a person close to Netanyahu some 10 days prior to Oct. 7.
"I'm certain that the issue of the early warnings on October 7 is going to continue to play with heightened emotions as we approach Election Day," said Novik. "This is going to be an indictment for history, not just for the elections."
Netanyahu has blamed Israeli security organizations for failing to stop the Oct. 7 attacks. He and his government have yet to establish a state commission of inquiry to investigate the failures around Oct. 7, despite public demand.
The new reports about warnings issued to Israel "actually turn the story on its head," pointing the finger right back at the prime minister, said Gayil Talshir, a political scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
"It violates the basic narrative that Netanyahu tries to tell Israelis," said Talshir.
NPR's Aya Batrawy contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Russia says plague institute worker's death does not risk an epidemic
articles.title_zh: Russia says plague institute worker's death does not risk an epidemic
articles.content_orig:
The victim was working at the anti-plague institute in the Siberia city of Irkutsk
US President Donald Trump has said he will speak with Vladimir Putin soon about the death of a lab worker at a plague research centre in Siberia.
"So far we are in very deep discussions," Trump said, adding that he would be able to report on his talks with the Russian leader "probably" on Thursday. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said no phone call had been scheduled.
Russian officials say they are investigating the cause of the 28-year-old's death and have not confirmed that the suspected disease is pneumonic plague. They insist there is no risk of an epidemic.
Mongolia has ordered "surveillance measures" on its border, AFP reports, while Lithuania has made preparations for any possible case.
Pneumonic plague is a serious lung infection, often described as the most virulent form of plague.
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for transparency from Russia.
"Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks," Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Putin's spokesman said Russia's reporting of the death to the WHO was in line with standard practice, and accused the media of reporting "false information".
The US has issued a formal diplomatic message to Russia requesting additional information. Peskov told reporters he was not aware of such a request.
Reports first emerged on Friday of almost 200 people being placed under observation in Siberia's Irkutsk region following the death.
The lab worker, named in Russian media as Darya Shipilova, had reportedly fallen ill a couple of days earlier.
Unconfirmed reports suggested that she had become ill after either breaking a test tube containing the pathogen at the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East where she worked or following a field trip to a region where plague occurs naturally among wild rodents.
As the US and the WHO sought more information, the country's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, issued a statement saying "there are no epidemic risks for the population of Irkutsk and the Irkutsk region".
It said more than 90% of the people who had been in contact with the victim had "completed medical observation" and "no health disorders associated with infectious pathology were detected".
Neighbouring Mongolia's government has ordered "health surveillance" measures on its border with Russia, AFP news agency reported. The country's health ministry said it would "maintain continuous surveillance and monitoring to prevent potential risks".
This was a precautionary measure, it said, adding "the current risk level is low."
Lithuania's health ministry said it has made preparations to manage any possible case in the country.
Laboratory testing is available, patients would be isolated in infectious disease hospitals, contacts would be identified, and the country has the stocks of medicines suitable for treatment, according to Nerija Kaulakien, an adviser at the Ministry of Health's Communications Division, in an interview with ELTA news agency.
There was no evidence of "an increased risk of plague" at the moment, she said.
In the immediate wake of the laboratory worker's death, Russia's health watchdog had issued a statement saying the woman had died of "pneumonia of an undetermined etiology" and that testing found "no microorganisms related to her professional activities".
However, after this announcement, a pro-government federal news outlet deleted five posts mentioning a possible plague case, and authorities in the town of Baikalsk deleted a message advising against travel to Shelekhov because of a possible plague infection.
Ongoing speculation into the lab worker's death has sparked a back and forth between Russia and the US, with questions about a possible spread outside of Russia.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US had "measures" available to help Russia if the situation turned out to be more serious than claimed.
According to the WHO, pneumonic plague has a very short incubation period - sometimes just 24 hours - and can be fatal, if not diagnosed and treated early.
People can be infected through:
contact with bodily fluids or contaminated materials
the inhalation of respiratory particles
Symptoms include shortness of breath and coughing, often with blood-tainted phlegm.
The bacterium that causes the plague, Yersinia pestis, found among rodents such as marmots in the area.
It killed up to half the population of Europe in the 14th Century when it was known as the Black Death .
It was in response to an outbreak in the 1920s that the Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East, was founded just over 100 years ago.

articles.title_orig: World’s largest steam locomotive returns to the rails for special holiday tour
articles.title_zh: World’s largest steam locomotive returns to the rails for special holiday tour
articles.content_orig:
For the first time since 2019, Union Pacific’s Living Legend No. 844 will be hitting the rails with Big Boy No. 4014. These historic locomotives will be together for a special holiday tour this November.
On November 21, the pair of steam locomotives will run during a fundraising tour from Greeley to Denver, Colorado. The trip will benefit the Make-A-Wish Foundation, with a donation from Union Pacific’s Community Ties Giving Program. The steam duo will also be on display to the public at Denver’s Union Station. Santa Claus and his elves will even be in the terminal handing out limited-edition gifts. Admission to this event is free and open to the public.
Tickets for the holiday fundraising tour to take a ride in vintage passenger cars pulled by Big Boy and No. 844 go on sale to patrons of the Union Pacific Railroad Museum on October 16. The general public can purchase any remaining tickets on October 19. Families can still visit Denver’s Union Station to view the locomotives free of charge.
Nicknamed the “Living Legend,” No. 844 is a famed high-speed passenger locomotive . It was built in 1944 and the last steam locomotive built for Union Pacific. It hauled some of the company’s most recognizable passenger trains, including the Overland Limited, Los Angeles Limited, Portland Rose, and Challenger . No. 844 is also the last Class I North American steam locomotive and never permanently retired from service. Instead, it was reassigned to freight service in Nebraska from 1957 to 1959, when diesel locomotives took over passenger service duties. Unlike nearly every other steam locomotive of its era, No. 844 escaped the scrap yard in 1960 and Union Pacific retained it for special service.
No. 844 will chug alongside a more famous locomotive, Big Boy No. 4014. Big Boy is currently the world’s largest operating steam locomotive and one of only eight remaining Big Boys in existence and the only one still in operation. These powerful locomotives were constructed during World War II to transport heavy equipment to support the war effort.
Earlier this year, Big Boy drew millions of spectators during a coast-to-coast journey celebrating the United States’ 250th birthday . The first leg began on March 29. Big Boy then traveled to several states including California, Utah, and New York.
The steam locomotive celebrated the Fourth of July in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania , where the Declaration of Independence was written in 1776. Thousands of train enthusiasts braved temperatures of 102 degrees Fahrenheit (with a real-feel of 112 degrees) to catch a glimpse of the 133-foot-long and 1.2-million-pound train.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | France Considers Issuing More Shorter-Term Debt After Bond-Market Turmoil
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | France Considers Issuing More Shorter-Term Debt After Bond-Market Turmoil
articles.content_orig:
France’s unprecedented wave of student protests has laid bare the country’s growing financial pressures, which will only become more difficult to tackle as Europe’s second-largest economy tries to rein in a ballooning budget deficit.
The country’s finances are in a precarious state. Public debt was more than $4 trillion in June, exceeding the size of the economy, according to the country’s statistics agency . The cost of servicing that debt has climbed by billions of dollars on last year, as bond yields spike .
At the same time, demands on the public purse are rising: Pension costs have climbed because of an aging population while the government looks to spend more on defense.
High school students, meanwhile, have called for a fix to staff shortages, overcrowded classrooms and crumbling school infrastructure.
Solutions to France’s financial troubles have led to social unrest in the past. Efforts to raise the retirement age sparked widespread protests in 2023 .
French school protests grow as workers join students
Last week, the French government proposed deep spending cuts and tax hikes aimed at narrowing the budget deficit, but bond buyers are concerned that fiscal measures may be watered down by lawmakers ahead of presidential elections next year, said Andrew Kenningham, chief European economist at consultancy Capital Economics.
The election could see President Emmanuel Macron ousted by either a far-right or far-left successor, raising questions over the country’s commitment to fiscal discipline. While Marine Le Pen’s right-wing National Rally recently proposed substantial spending cuts meant to stabilize the public finances, her party also remains committed to costly tax reductions, Kenningham said.
“Investors will also be concerned about greater fiscal populism after the elections,” he wrote in a note last week. “There is a big risk that spreads rise a lot further, either before or after next year’s elections.”
Worries about a potential debt crisis in France boiled over last week, leading to a selloff in French bonds and a sharp rise in yields.
The spread between French and German bond yields expanded to its widest level since 2012. That difference in yields means investors are demanding much higher returns to hold debt from France compared with Germany, which is deemed a safer alternative.
The French bond rout has sparked fears of spillovers to other high-yield European debt markets, with some analysts drawing parallels with the eurozone debt crisis of the early 2010s .
Global bond sell-off deepens, sending borrowing costs higher around the world
Given France’s size and systemic importance, “the potential for contagion into other countries and the Eurozone at large is very large and could potentially cause a serious crisis for the entire region,” Angel Talavera, chief European economist at Oxford Economics, an advisory firm, told CNN.
These worries in large part pushed the euro to its weakest level against the dollar since May 2025 on Monday. The currency, shared by 21 countries in the European Union, is worth around $1.12, having briefly dipped below that level.
The latest ructions in markets could weigh on a fragile economic recovery in Europe, bolstered by investment into artificial intelligence, stronger demand for European exports and higher defense spending in Germany.
Recent survey data showed that activity in manufacturing and services in the euro area increased at its fastest pace in nearly three-and-a-half years last month.
“(Economic) growth is staging a comeback and Europe has shown surprising resilience,” economists at Morgan Stanley wrote in a late September note.
Fall of yet another premier will make it hard for France to fix its finances. What’s behind its debt problem?
High bond yields are a clear risk to that growth, however.
If governments don’t cut spending , “interest rates will continue to go up,” Carsten Brzeski, head of macroeconomics at Dutch bank ING told CNN.
Higher bond yields push up the cost of borrowing throughout the economy, making home and car purchases more expensive and driving down investment. They also make it more expensive for governments to borrow money and force a certain degree of austerity to stop yields from rising further.
Yields on French, German and UK government bonds have broken multi-year records in recent weeks as concerns mount about the sustainability of public debt loads.
Europe’s public finances pose “serious risks to eurozone financial markets and to the economy,” Jack Allen-Reynolds, deputy chief eurozone economist at Capital Economics, told CNN.

articles.title_orig: World’s largest penguin colony suffers ‘enormous population crash’
articles.title_zh: World’s largest penguin colony suffers ‘enormous population crash’
articles.content_orig:
Chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski Island in Antarctica down by two-thirds since 2011, probably due to climate crisis
The world’s largest penguin colony has declined by two-thirds since 2011, most likely because of the climate crisis, a study has revealed.
Scientists said the rapid demise of chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski, the northernmost of the South Sandwich Islands in Antarctica , increased the risk of a wider ecosystem collapse.
“It is an enormous population crash, equivalent to half a million breeding individuals being lost from that island,” said the leader of the research, Prof Norman Ratcliffe, a penguin ecologist at the British Antarctic Survey .
The Guardian revealed in 2020 that chinstrap penguin populations were decreasing on Low in the South Shetland Islands, prompting concerns among scientists that “something is broken” in the world’s wildest ecosystem.
The new study, published on Wednesday in Current Biology, indicates that the speed of collapse may be accelerating so rapidly that the distinctive bird – which gets its name from a black line that runs below the beak from cheek to cheek – may need to be classified as an endangered species.
The island of Zavodovski had by far the biggest penguin colony in the world, with about 600,000 chinstraps and 90,000 macaroni penguins when the population was measured in 2011. Given the decline between then and 2025, it is likely to have lost that title to Cape Adare in the Ross Sea.
Scientists believe the most likely cause is climate disruption. Human-driven heating has pushed up winter temperatures on and around the Antarctic peninsula to 5C above preindustrial levels, one of the fastest rises in the world. On 6 June, the Argentinian Esperanza base on the Trinity peninsula registered a record winter high of 15.4C, about 20C above normal for the time of year – a margin that scientists described as “absolutely crazy”.
Chinstrap penguins are struggling to adapt because they have special diets and specific ocean temperature preferences. Tracking data shows they prefer to forage in cooler waters to the north-west of the island, where they would expect to find Antarctic krill, which make up the bulk of their diet. But as the waters warm, the krill have moved south into the Weddell Sea.
Macaroni penguins, by contrast, are less fussy eaters and their numbers rose 30% – though not nearly enough to make up for the loss of chinstraps. Ratcliffe said this was only small comfort because if current trends continued, all penguins would run out of space.
after newsletter promotion
He said the loss of chinstrap penguins would have wider repercussions for food webs. “Each ecosystem could be regarded as like a giant Jenga set, and every component that you remove increases the risk of ecosystems collapsing completely.”
The scientists ruled out several other possible causes of decline. There was no sign that chinstrap and macaroni penguins were in competition for food. The nearest humans lived thousands of miles away.
Although the island is volcanic and had a major eruption in 2016, prompting a “Penguin Pompeii hypothesis” of a sudden population fall , this theory was not borne out either by the data, which showed a steady linear decline, or by observations that showed the chinstraps avoided the main “asphyxia plain” area where the ash and lava were deposited.

The 2026 World Climbing Europe Youth Series concluded in Leipzig, Germany, on 3 October, with Speed medals awarded in the Under 17 and Under 19 age categories.
Austria, Poland and France shared the four gold medals, while the host nation collected three medals in total: one silver and two bronze.
UNDER 17 GOLDS FOR HASELWANTER AND MYŚLIWIEC
Austria’s Lara Haselwanter won the women’s Under 17 title in 7.30 seconds in the gold-medal race, as Slovenia’s Zoja Leskovar fell and took silver. Germany’s Lea Voigt secured bronze on home soil, clocking 9.08 against Italy’s Carolina Mariani, who also slipped and did not complete her race.

Eva-Lina Rymasz claimed women’s Under 19 gold for France, winning in 7.88 seconds ahead of Italy’s Alice Marcelli, who finished in 8.47. Ukraine’s Mariia Shymkova took bronze in 8.44 after Germany’s Mina Josephine Schultz slipped and fell in the bronze-medal race.
France’s Léo Grosset added men’s Under 19 gold to his country’s medal tally. Grosset clocked 5.23 in the final against Germany’s Mika Scherer, who fell but took silver. Switzerland’s Gilles Meili won bronze in 4.93 against fellow Swiss climber Sofiane Vial, who was unable to complete the race.

articles.title_orig: Rising seas threaten the world’s migratory shorebirds
articles.title_zh: Rising seas threaten the world’s migratory shorebirds
articles.content_orig:
Birds undertake some of the world’s most impressive migrations , travelling hundreds to thousands of kilometres every year in search of safe breeding grounds and seasonally abundant food resources. For many birds, migration is the key to their success . However, migration can also make species more vulnerable to threats.
Shorebirds — species that include sandpipers, plovers and oystercatchers — live and migrate along the world’s coastlines. Over the last several decades, coastal development has led to the loss of shorebird habitats in many areas of the world, driving population declines in multiple species . Now, a new threat is emerging: climate change-driven sea-level rise.
But how exactly does sea-level rise impact shorebirds, and just how serious is this threat?
Our new study reviews the evidence from 37 published papers to provide the first comprehensive overview of the threat of sea-level rise to the world’s shorebirds. Long story short: things aren’t looking good.
Shorebirds — as their name suggests — live along the shore, relying primarily on coastal ecosystems like  beaches, salt marshes and tidal flats. As sea levels rise, these vital habitats shrink.
Some coastal ecosystems may persist in the face of sea-level rise by moving inland with the rising waters, but this isn’t always possible. More than half of the world’s largest cities are within 100 kilometres of a coast , meaning that the presence of coastal infrastructure often blocks these pathways.
This leads to a phenomenon known as coastal squeeze — where ecosystems are increasingly squeezed between the rising waters and an inland barrier (such as dikes and seawalls built to protect homes and businesses), leading to decreases in habitat.
Loss of habitat has obvious implications for migratory shorebirds: less access to food, less space for nesting and more competition with other individuals.
But habitat loss isn’t the only threat to these species. Sea-level rise may also impact shorebirds in different ways, leading to changes in prey distribution , reproductive success , feeding time and many other factors.
Among the 37 studies that we examined, 21 predicted negative impacts of sea-level rise on shorebird habitats such as declines in habitat area or quality, while 17 predicted negative impacts on shorebird populations or individuals such as decreased survival or abundance.
Sea-level rise is expected to drive substantial habitat loss at many sites of international importance for migratory shorebirds. These include San Francisco Bay and Humboldt Bay in the United States, the Colorado River Delta and Marismas Nacionales in Mexico and the Yellow Sea region in East Asia, each of which supports 150,000 to more than one million shorebirds annually.
Habitat loss at these kinds of migratory bottleneck sites where large numbers of shorebirds congregate over a short period of time may hit populations particularly hard. Because so many birds funnel through these sites during migration, habitat loss in these areas may impact multiple species and entire populations. This means these sites must be a priority for conservation.
Maintaining coastal ecosystems and protecting them from the threat of sea-level rise will be essential for the survival of thriving shorebird populations. But coastal ecosystems aren’t only important for shorebirds. They also support thousands of other species and provide valuable ecosystem services such as coastal protection, water filtration and carbon storage.
In order to preserve these habitats and the species that depend on them, governments will need to make a serious effort to mitigate the impacts of coastal squeeze. Rather than continuing to armour our shorelines, decision makers should prioritize solutions that will protect human communities while also benefitting coastal ecosystems .
The shape that these actions take may vary from place to place. In some areas, it may be necessary to relocate coastal infrastructure to give ecosystems space to move inland as sea levels rise — an approach referred to as “managed retreat.” In other areas, scientists and practitioners are looking at how we can use sediment recovered from dredging to enhance or create new habitats.
However we choose to respond to sea-level rise, urgent action will be required to preserve shorebirds and their fascinating migrations for generations to come.

When Tony Fadell takes the stage at the inaugural MIT Future Fest , he projects a slide with three images of once-hyped AI devices that have already been discontinued: the Rabbit R1, the Humane Ai pin, and the Limitless pendant.
“These were kind of the ‘Gen 1’ AI products, and because of my background, these companies called me and asked me to help them,” Fadell said. “I didn’t.”
It’s no surprise that these companies want Fadell’s advice. He’s credited as the “father of the iPod,” a co-creator of the iPhone, and the founder of Nest, the smart thermostat company acquired by Google.
“You have to really understand what you’re trying to do, what pain you’re trying to solve,” he said. “In each of these cases, each one of them didn’t meet any kind of need — it was just interesting technology for geeks, and you’re like, ‘Okay, that’s neat, but it doesn’t really apply to my life.’”
These early AI devices promised the convenience of having a personal assistant, but didn’t actually work that well. Even if they did, most people have never had an assistant and know how they would use — or grow to trust — a personal robot helper.
“It’s less than 0.01% of the world population that has ever had a human [assistant] do anything, and so when [companies] say, ‘Oh, we want an assistant,’ that’s a bunch of people who have assistants saying it,” he said. “Most consumers don’t even know what an assistant is.”
Fadell goes on to explain to those of us in the 99.99% that hiring a trustworthy personal assistant isn’t as straightforward as pulling the most promising resume out of a pile of applications.
“It took me a couple of years first to understand how best to utilize [an assistant], and then to trust them with the most sensitive data, and have them be an agent where they’re setting up meetings with people and working with my bank,” he said. “I understand we have this vision of the future, but there’s a lot of steps to get the general consumer and even the general business on this path.”
It’s hard to talk about the struggles of building trust in your personal assistant without sounding a bit entitled, but Fadell has a point. When you hire a human assistant, you’re not giving them your bank account login on day one. We’re heading into a world where anyone can have a personal AI assistant, but these tools are only valuable if we can trust them to be completely secure.
At this point, establishing trust with an AI assistant seems even harder than relying on a human. Meta recently launched Muse , its all-purpose AI assistant, but users have reason to be wary. A security researcher quickly found a serious vulnerability in Muse after launch, and a recent 404 Media report states that some Meta employees discovered security issues that prompted multiple teams to embark upon a “mad dash” to fix these problems before launch, working overtime.
“Trust and safety are going to be paramount with anything that we turn over to some kind of intelligence,” Fadell said. “The only company I could see right now — maybe one other — is Apple who could do this. Apple has all the hardware, they have all the chips, they have all the pieces, but they don’t have all the AI stuff.”
Even if it’s not Apple that ultimately produces the stickiest AI agent, Fadell predicts that a successful agent will have to operate on-device only, both for the sake of privacy and to keep the tech lightweight.
“When you’re hearing all of these things about, ‘Oh, data centers are going to conquer the world,’ … I don’t believe it,” he said. “I’ve seen this before. I’ve seen this play out in the internet days and what have you. We have so much power on the device now, and even more compute, and they’re still battery operated.”
By keeping sensitive data on-device, rather than transmitting it through the cloud, Apple has garnered trust from users to share their biometric data through features like Face ID. As Fadell notes, Apple seems to have more goodwill with consumers than its competitors when it comes to privacy, but unlike other top tech companies, Apple doesn’t have a world-class AI model of its own — the new Siri AI runs on custom-built versions of Google’s Gemini.
While Apple lags in proprietary AI, it is leaps ahead in hardware. Fadell theorizes that companies like Meta and OpenAI are turning their attention toward gadgets because they don’t have billions of devices in circulation like Apple does.
“It’s because they don’t have access to the sensors on your phone. They’re like, ‘Oh, we’ll need video,’ and you have to check, ‘Yes, I’ll give you video.’ Then they say, ‘Well, we need audio.’ Check. ‘We need your GPS location.’ Check. And before you know it, it becomes a list of 20 things or more than you have then allowed them to have,” he said. “So what do they do? They go and make a device with all that stuff in it without a screen… and then they just Bluetooth or Wi-Fi into your phone and then back up to the web, or into a 5G network, so they can get all the sensor data.”
Given his history creating the iPhone and iPod, it might seem like Fadell is still looking at his former employer through rose-colored glasses. While he may give Apple credit where due, he hasn’t been shy to call Apple out when he thinks they’re messing up.
When an audience member asks about the luck involved in finding product-market fit, Fadell points out that it’s more difficult for startups to manufacture that luck, since a failed product can spell the end of the company.
“Because it’s a startup, you get one shot,” he quipped. “It’s not like Apple with the Vision Pro.”

articles.title_orig: WHO endorses lifestyle changes over GLP-1 drugs in child obesity fight
articles.title_zh: WHO endorses lifestyle changes over GLP-1 drugs in child obesity fight
articles.content_orig:
Children under 10 should not be given obesity drugs or GLP-1 weight-loss injections such as Mounjaro and Wegovy, new global guidelines from the World Health Organization say.
Most of these medications are only licensed for children or adolescents older than this, but some doctors prescribe them off-label, and drug companies are testing them in children as young as six.
WHO says the care should focus on healthy eating and exercise, not medicine or surgery, although they do not oppose drug trials.
Some digital technology, such as activity trackers and any online games that encourage the player to be more active and move, might be useful, it says, based on the limited evidence available.
Estimates suggest 170 million children and adolescents worldwide are obese.
That includes 70 million children aged 5–9. Obesity prevalence in this age group has quadrupled since 1990, rising from 2% to 8%.
In 2024, 35 million children under the age of five were overweight.
Obesity increases the risk of many different diseases, including type 2 diabetes.
Dr Luz De Rigil, Director of Nutrition and Food Safety at WHO, said: "For children under 10, WHO does not recommend obesity medicines, bariatric surgery or weight-management devices. This is a strong recommendation."
These might be appropriate for older children and adolescents when lifestyle approaches have failed and if the individual is "mentally and physically prepared" for the treatment, she added.
She said WHO recognises this is an evolving field and will continue to evaluate the evidence.
WHO's head of Nutrition and Food Safety Actions, Laurence Grummer-Strawn, said: "We are particularly concerned in this age group, if you are starting children very early on to using a GLP-1 or drugs like this, when does that stop?
"We don't really have evidence that you can use this as a temporary treatment and then turn to something dietary later on in life.
"We are very cautious about jumping in without clear evidence," he said.

The barriers to entry for game creation are rapidly diminishing as AI makes game development more accessible to people without traditional programming, design, or illustration skills. The latest example is an experiment from Google Labs.
On Wednesday, the tech giant’s public incubator and experimental platform launched a new AI-powered game-creation platform called Playground, which allows users to build browser-based games using simple text prompts, eliminating the need for coding expertise.
With Playground, creators can select a genre, such as trivia or racing, or start a project from scratch. They can specify whether they want a 2D or 3D game and choose between single-player and multiplayer experiences before describing the desired mechanics, gameplay, and visual style. Playground also allows users to upload visuals that its AI can transform into game assets tailored to the game’s overall art style.
Once created, games can be played on both mobile devices and computers. Projects can remain private, be shared through a link, or be published to Playground’s Explore gallery. Published games can support features such as leaderboards, while creators can continue modifying their projects even after they have been released.
Google also indicated that it plans to add Unity Spark integration in a future update. The integration could give Playground users access to additional 3D capabilities and “professional-level” game mechanics through Unity’s technology, further expanding what can be created through the platform.
Playground is initially available to users aged 18 and older in the U.S., with Google planning to expand availability to additional countries. Browsing and playing games in the catalog is free, while game generation relies on a weekly token system. The free tier provides a limited number of tokens, while Google One AI subscribers receive higher usage limits.
Google’s launch places Playground within a growing market of AI-assisted game-development tools. Roblox, for example, announced its own Build feature in July, enabling users to create games through natural-language prompts.
The initiative also builds on Google’s broader interest in gaming. The company previously explored cloud gaming through Stadia back in 2022, and later on continued incorporating games into other platforms, including YouTube Playables , a dedicated hub offering a selection of instantly playable web-based games.

articles.title_zh: World leaders solemnly mark 3 years since Oct. 7, as Hamas and Iran celebrate anniversary
articles.content_orig:

The world changed when Hamas attacked Israelis on Oct. 7, 2023 , catalyzing devastating conflict throughout the region . But within Israel, political sentiments have changed surprisingly little.
To some, the attack fulfilled long-term right-wing warnings that Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza would yield disaster; and the attack was incontrovertible proof that Palestinians will never live in peace with Israel.
Israeli left-wingers, for their part, have long held that a festering military rule over Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, and failure to reach peace, would inevitably lead to violent conflagration. For them, Oct. 7 only proved that they had been right all along.
The standoff raises crucial questions. In three years since Oct. 7, how has the attack changed Israeli society? And how will the answer affect upcoming elections in Israel?
To be sure, there have been cataclysmic changes in Israel, and the Middle East at large, since Oct. 7. The war in Gaza that began that day has become Israel’s longest war. A relatively stable ceasefire with Lebanon from 2006 to 2023 ended when Hezbollah, a Shi’a militia group, fired on Israel the day after Hamas’ attack; after multiple escalations since then, the current ceasefire is precarious. Israel and the U.S. have waged two full-blown wars with Iran, and the Middle East is still threatened by spin-off conflicts.
The losses Israelis suffered on Oct. 7 and since then have affected the country collectively and profoundly. For two years, many Israelis went from demonstration to demonstration demanding that their government prioritize a deal with Hamas to release Israeli hostages. Hundreds of thousands have spent the last three years in and out of active reserve duty.
Since 2023, Israel has seen record levels of emigration and growing international isolation. Sixty-one percent of Israelis told pollsters for the Israel Democracy Institute (IDI) that the national mood is poor .
Moreover, the destruction of Palestinian life and society , still ongoing , will one day force a terrible reckoning within Israel.
What’s less visible, and more surprising, is what has stayed the same. Israelis’ attitudes towards Palestinians, occupation, and conflict have become more extreme. But I would argue that Israeli public opinion today says much more about how Israel had changed prior to Oct. 7. The change in national attitudes since that fateful day has been moderate and consistent with what came before.
In December 2022, almost a year before Oct. 7, support for peace through a two-state solution hit a historic low. In the joint Palestinian-Israeli survey I conduct together with colleagues at Tel Aviv University and the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research, support stood at 39% of Israelis that year—the lowest since the 1990s. Among Jewish respondents, just 34% supported a two-state solution, and 37% believed Israel should permanently annex the West Bank while Palestinians would have limited rights.
When we conducted the study again in mid-2024, Jews were twice as likely to support a single, Israeli-dominated unequal state as they were to support two states.
Palestinian attitudes in 2022 were similar. Just one-third supported two states. Both sides showed a mirror-image majority who distrusted the other. In surveys by the IDI from that same time, 59% of Jewish Israelis defined themselves as right-wing; just 12% said they were left-wing.
What changed after Oct. 7? This July, the Tel Aviv University Peace Index survey found that support for two states stood at 31%, an eight-point decline in the four years since 2022. Now, IDI surveys find that just over 60% of Israeli Jews describe themselves as right-wing, just a few points higher than late 2022.
Israel has changed, but this change began years before Oct. 7 2023. In 2010 , no fewer than 71% of Israelis supported a two-state solution in the joint surveys. The years that followed were plagued by stagnation and dissipation of any peace process, regular wars with Hamas, and a heavily nationalist government in Israel. It stands to reason that these phenomena pushed Israeli society further to the right. Support for the two-state solution eroded slowly, then rapidly by the end of the decade.
That shift was self-reinforcing: the more right-wing Israelis became (primarily the Jewish population), the more elected leaders took ever-more radical positions such as supporting settlement expansion and de facto annexation in the West Bank. In 2019, Prime Minister Netanyahu began referring to extending sovereignty over parts of the West Bank, or de jure annexation . The current government accelerated those processes drastically.
Study after study shows that Arab citizens of Israel have remained the strongest supporters of peace, before and after the current wars. But with Jewish Israeli and Palestinian attitudes so dismal in the years before Oct. 7, the chances of resurgent violence almost seemed inevitable.
In other words, most Israelis did not radically transform their worldview after Oct. 7. In fact, hardline political trends were among the many factors contributing to the terrible escalation to begin with.
Another thing that hasn’t changed in Israel during the last three years of war: hopes for peace. The number of Israeli Jews who self-describe as left-wing has barely shifted. In a May survey for the Institute for National Security Studies, about 20% of the total population, Jews and Arabs, define themselves as left-wing, and a similar share typically say they are centrist. These groups embrace a commitment to democracy, liberal values, separation of religion and state, and reject the religious fundamentalism of the current government.
The left remains committed to peace via diplomacy and Palestinian self-determination. In a mid-2025 survey I conducted for a peace organization called A Land for All, where I am also an active member, the large majority of self-defined left-wing Israelis, and nearly half of centrists, supported a basic two-state solution.
Do peace attitudes even matter, when there is no peace process? That may be theoretical for now, but elections aren’t. Israelis will be voting on Oct. 27. Polls show the voters deeply divided , just as they were in the elections held between 2019 and 2022.
Netanyahu’s far-right coalition is not doing well. Nearly all polls show his coalition parties well below their actual result in 2022. And most mainstream polls show a consistent majority for today’s opposition parties.
At first glance, these shifts might seem antithetical. Aren’t these ideological and electoral trends moving in contradictory directions: more right-wing, but a majority against the current government?
It turns out that even the Israeli electoral contradiction is not new. During the five elections from 2019 through 2022, a majority of Israelis were right-wing and voted for right-wing parties. But to form a coalition, some of those parties no longer supported Netanyahu and refused to join a coalition under his leadership. Netanyahu therefore commanded only about half the seats in parliament following four of these cycles. Neither side had a clear or firm coalition majority, and the country was thrown into electoral turmoil five times over.
But if all mainstream polls show the anti-Netanyahu parties winning, including right-wing opposition parties, shouldn’t that mean a decisive outcome against him this time? Not quite: no poll shows Israel’s Jewish, Zionist parties reaching a majority in October.
And in Israel’s right-wing, populist discourse, the main opposition party leaders opposed to Netanyahu now, Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman, with similar statements from frontrunner Gadi Eisenkot , insist that parties representing Arab citizens must not be part of a coalition after Oct. 7. Two seaside resorts in New England are among the best on the planet, according to Conde Nast Traveler readers.
The travel publication released a list of the 50 best resorts in the world on Tuesday, part of its 39th Annual Readers’ Choice Awards , and Chatham Bars Inn in Chatham ranked No. 18. Weekapaug Inn in Westerly, R.I. ranked No. 28.
Chatham Bars Inn , which was also named the No. 1 resort in New England , is “a benchmark of luxury on the Cape,” Conde Nast Traveler wrote.
“If you’re looking for a full-service resort with all the bells and whistles and then some, this is it, including an eight-acre private farm to stock the resort’s numerous dining and drinking outlets; one of the better spas on the Cape; an expansive pool deck with F&B service; a private quarter-mile beachfront; tennis courts with lessons available; and a 24-hour gym,” wrote the publication.
Resort officials celebrated on social media , writing, “Thank you to our incredible team and to our guests and supporters who voted for us. We’re grateful to be recognized alongside so many remarkable destinations.”
Weekapaug Inn, also named the No. 2 resort in New England , is a historic getaway in Rhode Island.
“A recently renovated legendary seaside inn on the National Register of Historic Places, the 27-room, six-suite Weekapaug Inn is a three-hour drive from New York and less than two from Boston—ideal for a quick weekend jaunt,” wrote Conde Nast Traveler .
Visitors enjoy guided nature walks, golf, tennis, and boating expeditions in historic vessels, noted the publication.
Officials at Weekapaug Inn also shared their excitement on social media , writing, “Thank you to the Condé Nast Traveler readers who voted, and to our incredible teams for truly delivering the best of service, cuisine, and luxury, year after year. We hope to share our award-winning experiences with you soon.”
The No. 1 resort in the world is Cheval Blanc Seychelles, according to Conde Nast Traveler readers.
This year, Conde Nast Traveler readers cast 798,867 votes for the annual awards, determining the very best in hotels, resorts, spas, airlines, and more worldwide. The results will be featured in the magazine’s November issue.

articles.title_orig: US 30-year mortgage rate hits highest in nearly three years
articles.title_zh: US 30-year mortgage rate hits highest in nearly three years
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates have hit their highest level in almost three years, making buying a home more challenging at a time when housing prices are already high. Nam Y. Huh/AP hide caption
Carrie Goldstein's dream for a new home started with a family reunion at her cousin's home in Milwaukee. The home was old with character and she could walk anywhere from the front door.
"We were kind of in awe and drooling over her walkability," Goldstein says.
It was the lifestyle Goldstein wanted but lacked in her Cleveland suburb, which she says is also pretty walkable – with one major issue.
"There are lots of sidewalks," she says. "But you can't really go anywhere."
She brainstormed with her husband and realized nearby Rocky River was where they wanted to live. It was still a suburb, but with a quaint downtown and the option to walk to Lake Erie.
But as much as she wanted to move, one thing stopped her cold. The mortgage she would have to pay. Mortgage rates have hit their highest level in almost three years, making buying a home impossible for many people at a time when housing prices are also sky high.
Goldstein is running into a problem that's affecting many households at a time when people have already been struggling with years of high inflation: The rising cost of borrowing.
Carrie Goldstein stands outside her home on October 4, 2026. Home prices and mortgage rates prevent her from moving. Mike Goldstein hide caption
Bond markets influence all types of borrowing costs across the economy – and as yields have surged to their highest in decades, they've pushed up all kinds of interest rates paid by consumers, from loans for homes to cars and higher education.
And those rates are likely to continue moving up after the Federal Reserve in September raised interest rates for the first time this year – while signaling an additional hike could come this year.
Rate hikes from the Federal Reserve filter through the economy and are meant to slow down consumer and business spending by making people hesitant to take out a more expensive loan to pay for a car or a home – both essential purchases for many people.
"If you need to borrow, boy, it's really not a good time," says John Diamond, senior director of the Center for Tax and Budget Policy at the Baker Institute.
Buying a home is a key example of how households are affected when borrowing costs rise in the economy.
While mortgage rates were falling at the start of this year, they reversed upward after the U.S. war with Iran spooked the bond market by raising worries about inflation. As a result, mortgage rates, which are influenced by the bond markets, have surged this year.
For example, at the current 7.28% level for the average 30-year fixed rate mortgage, a person could end up paying about $900 more a month compared with the 3% pandemic-era rates for a median priced home.
As expected, fewer homeowners are willing or capable of making that financial leap, even if they have long since outgrown their current home. Existing house sales in August were down about 1.2% from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors.
It's not just mortgage costs that are making Americans like Goldstein wince.
Alongside her dreams of owning a home in a walkable neighborhood, Goldstein is ready for a new car. Her old one is 11 years old, has 150,000 miles and plenty of quirks. The repair costs are approaching the point where they'll be more than the value of the actual car.
But a four-year loan for a used car is about three percentage points higher compared with the start of 2022, right around when auto loans began to shed their pandemic-era low rates and started climbing up.
"You can't go and get a car for $150 or $180 bucks anymore a month," she says about the car payments she would be facing.
Although so far the Fed has only delivered a modest quarter of a percentage point, it's adding to the higher borrowing costs at a time when households are already dealing with inflation and higher prices for other types of borrowing.
"It's added to higher mortgage payments. Higher student loan payments. Higher prices because of inflation," Diamond says. "That's what makes it really painful."
And that could mean that households could continue to delay any big purchases requiring a loan.
Goldstein is one of them. She says she can afford to wait on the car and house. But eventually she unsubscribed from real estate updates for that walkable suburb.
"It just became more and more disheartening when I did the math," Goldstein says. "It's just not in the cards."
