articles.title_orig: IceCube, high-energy neutrinos, and Francis Halzen win 2026’s Physics Nobel
articles.title_zh: IceCube, high-energy neutrinos, and Francis Halzen win 2026’s Physics Nobel
articles.content_orig:
Credit : Bryce Richter / UW–Madison
An astrophysics column on big questions and our universe.
There’s a whole entire Universe out there, and the more we learn about it as it actually is, the greater our potential becomes to achieve great things as a civilization, even if the path from knowledge to improving humanity is far from clear. The Nobel Prize was set up more than 100 years ago with the express purpose of rewarding those whose work provides the “greatest benefit to humankind” in a number of disciplines, including physics. We couldn’t foresee that:
Similarly, we cannot know what advances will arise in the future from advances made today in fields like elementary particle physics, gravitational waves, or neutrino astronomy, but possibilities range from computational advances to superior timekeeping technologies to extraterrestrial communication. One thing is certain, however: we have to make the fundamental advance, first, if we ever hope to find out. In many ways, that’s what the science of physics is all about.
It’s for that reason that the world ought to be incredibly excited that the 2026 Nobel Prize in physics has gone to Francis Halzen , for “decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin,” which is a remarkable testament to what a single individual can accomplish with a creative idea, a lot of hard work and organization, persistence, a strong national investment in science, and quite a bit of good luck. Here’s the story of this remarkable advance in neutrino physics and astrophysics.
The idea of IceCube was born 39 years ago, back before “neutrino astrophysics” was a field that went beyond our Solar System. Prior to 1987, neutrino astrophysics was restricted solely to measuring the neutrinos coming from within the Solar System: by building a large tank of fluid deep underground. Starting in 1968 , the idea was that neutrinos from the Sun, occasionally, would interact with an atomic nucleus, transmuting a neutron into a proton, and converting the neutrino into an electron in the process. By looking for the newly transmuted nuclei, solar neutrinos could then be detected.
In principle, nuclear reactions would occur all across the Universe, releasing neutrinos when they did, but the flux would be far too low to detect them. However, due to contemporaneous interest in grand unified theories , particle physicists had begun building much larger tanks of fluid surrounded by photomultiplier tubes, with the idea being to detect any spontaneously decaying protons by measuring their faster-than-light in the liquid medium radiation: Cherenkov radiation .
The major experiment of the 1980s, Kamiokande , was originally an experiment to search for nucleon decay in Kamioka, Japan. Running for several years, it only obtained null results, until the day of February 24, 1987. All of a sudden, an array of signals emerged: 12 of them (antineutrinos, technically) in the Kamiokande II detector alone . Four hours later, the light arrived as well, confirming this was indeed a supernova event. Kamiokande, the Kamioka nucleon decay experiment, kept the same acronym, but renamed itself to the Kamioka neutrino detector experiment. From a failed search for proton decay , the science of neutrino astronomy was born.
Over the subsequent years and decades, most approaches to neutrino detection simply scaled up this approach. Large, underground, liquid-filled detectors lined with photomultiplier tubes optimized to detect Cherenkov radiation were the key to building neutrino detectors, including Super-Kamiokande and the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory (SNOLab), where the original research led to a Nobel Prize awarded in 2002 for neutrino physics and the upgraded research led to one in 2015 for neutrino oscillations.
However, in the aftermath of the 1987 supernova and subsequent neutrino detection, Francis Halzen began thinking about a different approach. Giant tanks were fundamentally limited in a key way: the effective volume available for interactions with neutrinos was constrained to be no larger than the size of your tank. If you wanted to find rare events, your only options were to either build a larger tank or to wait for longer periods of time, until such a neutrino from a rare event happened to interact within your detector.
Halzen came up with an alternative in 1988, which he merely (and humbly) referred to as a “cute idea,” which was to do away with a photomultiplier tube-lined tank entirely. Instead, he wondered, given that there’s so much ice located at the Earth’s south pole, could one simply use Antarctic ice as the “detector” for interacting with neutrinos instead?
Of course, it wouldn’t be possible or practical to use the entire Antarctic ice sheet, but Halzen realized that if you restricted yourself to a mere section of it — a large, cubical block — you could vastly increase the potential interaction volume over what you could ever hope to build with a conventional, liquid-filled and photomultiplier tube-lined detector. If it could be implemented successfully, Halzen’s vision could bring about a neutrino detector that was able to see events that were far rarer than the other neutrino detector designs would be sensitive to.
We had a longstanding hint of this from cosmic rays: non-neutrino particles (mostly protons, but also some heavier nuclei) that struck and interacted with Earth’s upper atmosphere, producing energetic particle showers. Sometimes, the daughter particles emerging from the shower could be detected directly on the ground, but most frequently, the shower of particles would interact with the Earth’s atmosphere: moving faster-than-light in the medium of air, and producing a cone of blue light that was once again the hallmark of Cherenkov radiation. Arrays of Cherenkov telescopes routinely detect this light, and reconstruct the signatures (and energies) of the particles that originally created them. When they do, they find that there are cosmic particles out there far, far more energetic than anything we could ever hope to realistically produce in laboratory experiments here on Earth.
If these high-energy particles — albeit, rare particles — are out there in the Universe, ostensibly created by high-energy sources like neutron stars, black holes, and active quasars, then it stands to reason that similar processes will create ultra-energetic neutrinos as well. However, since the number of particles above a given energy rapidly decreases as a function of energy, it would also imply that ultra high-energy neutrino events should be exceedingly rare as well, requiring enormous volumes of “detector material” in order to even see one or a few of them.
Super-Kamiokande is the world’s largest operational neutrino detector tank, holding just over 50,000 tonnes of extraordinarily pure water, but is only about 40 meters on a side. (Technically, in a cylindrical shape.) For comparison, however, if you went deep into the Antarctic ice, you should be able to find ice that is:
Halzen’s idea was to use hot water to bore cylindrical holes straight down into the Antarctic ice at regularly spaced intervals, and then to place specialized Cherenkov detectors down deep within the ice itself, filling the gaps back up with water to restore the ice back to its pristine, block-like state. If these detectors were spaced out over a volume of ice that was a cubic kilometer in size — 1 km × 1 km × 1 km — it would possess 20,000 times the detection volume of Super-Kamiokande!
The prototype for what would become the IceCube neutrino detector was known as AMANDA: the Antarctic Muon And Neutrino Detector Array . AMANDA was made up of optical modules — each with one photomultiplier tube inside to be sensitive to Cherenkov light — that were sunk into the Antarctic ice beneath the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station. articles.title_orig: The world’s oyster reefs could add $12 trillion to planetary health each year – if they were better managed
articles.title_zh: The world’s oyster reefs could add $12 trillion to planetary health each year – if they were better managed
articles.content_orig:
Scientists calculated the total gross ecosystem product that the world’s oyster reefs could deliver to planetary health and human wellbeing, given adequate interventions for habitat restoration and protection. They estimated that the combined potential ecosystem services of oyster reefs, including food production, carbon sequestration, water filtration, and coastline protection, could be worth up to $12 trillion per year. For this potential to be realized, 90% of sites suitable for oyster reefs would require restoration, while 80% would need protection through conservation efforts.
A new study shows that the world’s oyster reefs are a precious resource that’s vastly underestimated and underutilized. The authors set out to calculate the reefs’ potential gross ecosystem product (GEP), the ecological counterpart of the gross economic product, and arrived at trillions of dollars of ecosystem goods and services delivered each year to different aspects of planetary health, including human wellbeing. But for their full potential to be realized, oyster reefs around the world will need to be restored and protected.
“Here we estimate that fully restored oyster reefs in the top ten hotspot countries worldwide would yield a GEP of $12 trillion,” said Dr Matteo Convertino, an associate professor at Tsinghua University and the corresponding author of the publication in Frontiers in Marine Science .
The UN’s Sustainable Development Goal ‘Life below water’ calls for the conservation and sustainable use of coastal and marine resources to safeguard human wellbeing. But today, oyster reefs — like all coastal ecosystems — are under growing pressure from overexploitation, pollution, and climate change. Worldwide, an estimated 85% of such reefs have been lost over the past century, especially in estuaries and river deltas.
Convertino and colleagues began by assessing where suitable habitats for oyster reefs exist around the world today and where reefs could spontaneously form, given the right protection and interventions for restoration. They then estimated the potential value of the entire ‘portfolio’ of ecosystem services these reefs could deliver. Besides oysters for human consumption, these include water filtration, shoreline protection, the recycling of nutrients through the food web, and carbon sequestration. Oyster reefs also provide food, shelter, and nursery grounds for a plethora of fish and invertebrates.
Read and download the original article
The scientists imported thousands of geotagged records of oyster reefs from two public databases. They then used a tried-and-tested machine learning algorithm to predict geographic distributions and habitat suitability around the world, and identify potential new locations for reefs. Their estimate of suitability weighed a slew of environmental measures such as local water temperature, salinity, light, nutrient-richness, and oxygenation. Any location with a habitat suitability score of 65% or greater was classified as suitable. By combining a given area’s score with a measure of the ecosystem services that a reef there could provide, the authors rated the ‘ecopotential’ of each location. The higher the ecopotential, the greater the potential benefit.
The results showed that the predicted ecopotential is greatest in ten ‘hotspot nations’: the US, Australia, Chile, China, Japan, South Korea, Argentina, France, Germany, and Italy. Across these countries, approximately 295,000 square kilometers, or 6% of their coastal zones, were deemed to be suitable. Oyster reefs are currently known to occupy only 10% of this area, mainly in lagoons and bays, estuaries, and river deltas: this indicates that there is a lot of room for expansion. Importantly, only 23% of the suitable area is currently under any form of marine protection.
If the entire area with positive ecopotential were occupied by reefs, the authors’ calculations show that these could filter prodigious volumes of water: 77.58 quadrillion liters in the US, 69.92 quadrillion liters in Australia, and 46.58 quadrillion liters in Chile. These reefs could also sequester as much as 12.3 million metric tons of carbon a year. In the US alone, the combined potential value of nitrogen removal, carbon sequestration, and water purification by oyster reefs was estimated at $25.1 billion a year.
However, the authors stressed that these are estimates, which infer ecosystem services from global averages of key parameters, and which could be affected by changes in oyster populations over time or by the climate crisis. Significant work on habitat restoration and protection would also be needed to unlock reefs’ potential.
“We estimated that 90% of sites suitable for oyster reefs require restoration, while 80% need protection through conservation efforts. In other words, the current oyster situation is very suboptimal but there is a huge opportunity, considering the benefits,” said Convertino.
“Because global warming generally decreases the habitat quality of oyster reefs, we expect that their global GEP will go down from the current potential value of $12 trillion. But some countries may see an expansion of reefs due to more favorable conditions for the growth and dispersal of oysters: in particular this could happen in Australia, Indonesia, South Korea, Japan, and France.”

articles.title_orig: Former German intelligence chief arrested on espionage charges
articles.title_zh: Former German intelligence chief arrested on espionage charges
articles.content_orig:
A former head of Germany 's foreign intelligence service was arrested on Tuesday on suspicion that he had passed state secrets to a foreign intelligence service, the federal prosecutor's office said.
August Hanning, who led the Federal Intelligence Service, known by its German acronym BND, from 1998 to 2005, is “strongly suspected of treasonous espionage, spying out state secrets, attempted treason, and espionage,” the federal prosecutor’s office said in a statement.
Hanning, 80, was arrested at his home in Norwalde near the city of Münster in Northwestern Germany. A former aide, identified as Manfred D, was also arrested on Tuesday in Bad Tölz in Southern Bavaria and has been charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage. Following federal court hearings on Tuesday and Wednesday both men have been remanded in custody.
“In one instance, there is suspicion that Mr. Hanning used classified information to prepare an analysis for an employee of a foreign intelligence service,” Ines Peterson, a spokesperson for the federal prosecutor’s office, told German media outlets.
“In another instance, he is alleged to have passed on information following an extensive exchange — also with an employee of another intelligence service.”
Neither Peterson nor the earlier statement by the prosecutor's office revealed who exactly the two men were suspected of spying for or which foreign intelligence services they provided with classified information. Premises belonging to both men were searched late on Tuesday.
“The federal government takes this case extremely seriously and is providing full support to the investigating authorities,” a spokesperson for German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told reporters Wednesday.
The prosecutor's office said Manfred D. worked as Hanning's chief of staff and later served as chief of staff for several subsequent BND presidents from 2012 until 2026. “In his role, he had access to confidential information,” the prosecutor's office said.
Both suspects are believed to have agreed in 2010 to have Manfred D. continuously transmit valuable intelligence from the BND to Hanning in exchange for payment, the statement said.
“The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D. provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the federal intelligence service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings,” the statement said.
Hanning used the information in private consulting work and Manfred D., who in line with German privacy rules cannot be identified by his full name, provided Hanning with classified information until June 2022, Peterson said.
Hanning came under scrutiny in a separate investigation into the abduction of Hamburg businesswoman Christina Block’s children from her ex-husband in Denmark in January 2024 in a lengthy custody battle. The investigation into that case led to Tuesday's arrests.
The current proceedings stem from evidence found during a search of Hanning’s residence in connection with the abduction case, the federal prosecutor’s office stated.
Hanning and a retired official from the Hamburg State Criminal Police Office are suspected of having accepted a contract from the businesswoman in 2022 to abduct her children while serving as executives of a security firm, the public prosecutor’s office announced in the fall of 2025, according to German news agency dpa.
The Blocks are a prominent Hamburg family best known for their popular national steakhouse chain ‘Block House’. The custody trial has received a lot of attention in the country, with German tabloids offering heavy coverage from the court.
German opposition lawmaker Konstantin von Notz expressed shock about the allegations against Hanning and called for a quick investigation.
“This is a hard-hitting and deeply troubling story,” said von Notz, a member of the Greens party and also the German parliament committee overseeing the intelligence services.
“We expect a swift and thorough investigation into the egregious allegations levelled against former BND chief Hanning,” he said.
Van Notz also called on the German state to bar former top executives and those with top level security clearances from engaging in private consultancy work after vacating office, a matter he classified of national security interest.

articles.title_orig: Doja Cat’s ‘Tour Ma Vie World Tour’ tests her performer bona fides
articles.title_zh: Doja Cat’s ‘Tour Ma Vie World Tour’ tests her performer bona fides
articles.content_orig:
When an artist abandons the standard fanfare and extravagance of an arena tour, their true performance ability is put to the test. Doja Cat’s “Tour Ma Vie World Tour” demonstrated her showmanship needs no hefty entourage of backup dancers, elaborate sets or choreography.
The tour, which hit Chicago’s United Center on Oct. 3, traverses the R&B artist’s ’80s-infused 2025 album “Vie,” while incorporating older hits like “Need to Know” and “Say So.” Apart from a handful of male backup dancers and occasional pyrotechnics, her tour is largely an understated affair as she commands the audience’s attention almost entirely on her own.
Opening with a hearty brass interlude, Doja Cat began the evening with “Cards,” the first track on “Vie.” Her performance evoked sartorial themes of the ’80s, as she donned pink geometric yoga pants and a bright orange cheetah-patterned coat. Vibrant lighting punctuated the disco-heavy setlist as Doja Cat ventured further into the album, which combines dance-pop and disco.
Her newest album and its accompanying tour are quite a departure for Doja Cat, whose earlier discography is primarily contemporary R&B and rap.
While the show’s runtime focused heavily on “Vie,” Doja Cat gained substantial mileage from older hits like “Need to Know” from her 2021 album “Planet Her” and “Streets” from her 2019 album “Hot Pink,” a testament to her artistic depth.
The concert presents Doja Cat at her most comfortable, highlighting the signature unseriousness that makes her such a compelling performer. At one point, she playfully lit a cigarette before jumping back into song. Later on, she pied an audience member in the face during a tongue-in-cheek interactive skit.
Though there were scattered moments of grandeur, Doja Cat was at her best when she was alone onstage, commanding the audience without flashy costume changes or theatrical gimmicks.
The most memorable track from the evening was unequivocally “Paint The Town Red,” a hit from her 2023 album “Scarlet.” Unaccompanied by background vocals, Doja Cat exerted a larger-than-life stage presence throughout the track, eliciting deafening cheers from the audience.
True to form, Doja Cat concluded the concert on a high note, launching a pyrotechnics show to close out the night and putting her band centerstage for an epic guitar solo. Bouncing between fan favorites like “Tia Tamera” and new songs like “Stranger,” the artist underscored her thematic versatility as a performer.
Though her performance was notably unostentatious, Doja Cat’s “Tour Ma Vie World Tour” proves she is a born performer. With a refined yet metamorphic style, Doja Cat demonstrated she can be as dynamic as she is iconic.

articles.title_orig: Susan Collins vs. Troy Jackson: 5 takeaways from Maine Senate debate
articles.title_zh: Susan Collins vs. Troy Jackson: 5 takeaways from Maine Senate debate
articles.content_orig:
Republican challenged by Democrat Troy Jackson in critical Senate race says she opposes Iran war and Canada tariffs
Susan Collins, the Republican senator for Maine , pointedly distanced herself from Donald Trump in a televised debate with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson on Tuesday, as she sought to present an image of independence in a state that has voted against Trump three times.
Proclaiming herself as not the US president’s “favorite senator”, Collins made the highly unusual boast for a Republican that she had voted with Joe Biden, a Democrat, more than 90% of the time when he was president. She also emphasized her differences with her fellow Republicans , saying she voted against her own party more than any other senator.
Collins’s defensiveness came amid a determined onslaught from Jackson, 58, a veteran former state legislator who was getting his first chance to present himself to a broad audience since replacing Graham Platner as the Democratic candidate in a contest that could be vital to the party’s hopes of winning the Senate.
Platner, a former harbor master, was forced to withdraw from the race in July after facing sexual assault allegations, which he denied, leaving Democrats racing against the clock to replace a candidate who had built up momentum campaigning on a populist progressive platform.
Jackson painted Collins as a Trump loyalist, saying she voted with the president 96% of the time. He also doggedly focused on her 2018 vote for the conservative supreme court justice Brett Kavanaugh, tying it to the court’s subsequent overturning of Roe v Wade, which had for half a century guaranteed the national right to abortion.
“Tonight is about who you stand with when it matters,” Jackson said in a pithy opening statement. “Eight years ago today, Maine women went to DC and begged Senator Collins not to confirm Brett Kavanaugh, but she did it anyways.
“He helped overturn Roe v Wade, and today she says she has no regrets. Would you trust her to pick the next supreme court justice?”
Collins, 73, who has been a senator since 1996, has frequently presented herself as a moderate who stands against more radical trends in her own party. The posture is in line with Maine’s profile as a more Democratic-leaning state, which Trump has not won in any of his three presidential campaigns and which has voted for Democratic presidential candidates in every election since 1992.
Nevertheless, Collins went to unusual lengths to differentiate herself from Trump on a range of issues, including the war with Iran, which she said she voted to end nine times, calling it “not well thought out”.
Collins reacted with something close to alarm when the moderator, Gregg Lagerquist, said Trump had suggested that the president might pay a campaign visit to Maine.

“I don’t think that President Trump is going to come to Maine,” she said. “He’s talking about going to a lot of different states. I’ve heard nothing from his office, and I’m not exactly his favorite senator.”
Collins stressed her differences with the president on specific issues pertinent to the Maine economy, including rural healthcare and tariffs against Canada, with which the state shares a border.
“I have been the most outspoken opponent of the tariffs on Canada,” she said. “Canada is not China. It’s our neighbor and our friends.”
Polls show the two candidates running neck and neck.

articles.title_zh: FlyDubai Attacker Was Part of Pilot Hiring Spree at Fast-Growing Airline
articles.content_orig:
An Israeli airline El Al aircraft is parked on the tarmac at Ben Gurion Airport near the city of Lod on Friday. Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
TEL AVIV, Israel — An ongoing investigation into last week's midair attack on a FlyDubai plane has found that the co-pilot who tried to take control of the flight intended to crash it into Israel's Ben Gurion International Airport, a person familiar with the matter but not authorized to speak publicly told NPR.
The plane was flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv and was intending to land at Ben Gurion midmorning on a busy weekday. The co-pilot attacked the plane's captain midflight with an axe and attempted to take control of the plane.
It is believed that the co-pilot likely acted alone, the source said.
Authorities in the United Arab Emirates — which is leading the main investigation into the incident, with help from Israeli officials — and in Israel have deemed the attack an attempted terrorist attack, although the motive is still being investigated.
The commercial flight had 172 people on board, according to the airline, the majority of whom were Israeli. All passengers and crew were safe and accounted for after the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. They were flown to Tel Aviv late Wednesday.
Investigators said that the co-pilot carried out the attack with what's called a crash axe — a lightweight emergency tool stored in the cockpit to break through panels or jammed doors in the event of a crash.
The aviation tracking site Flightradar24 said data shows at one point the plane descended more than 14,000 feet, or nearly 3 miles, in under 30 seconds — way faster than normal.
The pilot was able to open the cockpit door during the attack, and passengers rushed in and subdued the attacker, while another pilot who happened to be on board helped land the plane, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who spoke to the injured pilot as he was recovering in the hospital.
Both the pilot and the co-pilot are alive and have been transferred to the UAE for questioning.
The co-pilot is from Oman, according to Israeli officials. Omani and Emirati officials have not confirmed that publicly.
The detail of his nationality is raising questions in Israel about how he was allowed to fly a plane heading to Ben Gurion, as Israel does not allow pilots from countries it doesn't have diplomatic relations with to fly in its airspace. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Fox & Friends that Israel checks the background of pilots flying routes into the country, and that the attacker must have gotten through a "loophole."
Officials from Israel's Ministry of Transportation and security services have traded accusations over the lack of oversight and vetting of the pilot. Meanwhile, several of Netanyahu's political opponents have said the security breach is a failure on the prime minister's part and have called for a larger investigation.
Netanyahu announced late Sunday that there will be a formal examination into the security situation around "foreign civil aviation into Israel," but did not provide further details.
National elections in Israel — which will determine whether or not Netanyahu will remain prime minister — are just weeks away. It's the first such national election since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, which sparked the war in Gaza.
Polls in Israel show that the race is tight, and analysts say the FlyDubai attack would likely not change Israelis' attitudes on how they will vote.
Netanyahu has been campaigning largely on the idea that he alone can protect Israelis from the external threats that Israel faces, while his opponents have pointed to what they see as major security failures under his leadership — including the Oct. 7 attack.

articles.title_zh: Germany news: Far-right AfD gets first house speaker in a German state parliament
articles.content_orig:
This blog has now closed. Read below for a look at the latest news stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, October 6, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Germany plans to buy four more Meko A-200 frigates from TKMS for about €5.6 million   ($6.3 billion), the Reuters news agency reported on Tuesday, citing a Finance Ministry document.
The country's parliamentary budget committee is expected to approve the purchase on Thursday, with the construction due to be finalized by 2035, as per Finance Ministry documents seen by Reuters.
Defense Minister Boris Pistorius had cancelled a rival F126  frigate project with Dutch company Damen , over delays and cost overruns.
Germany’s far-right AfD party took a significant step toward exercising political power in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
One month after winning 44% of the regional vote, the party secured the presidency of the state parliament, with Tobias Rausch elected as speaker of the house.
What does this moment mean for Germany? DW reports from Magdeburg.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Parliamentarians in Saxony-Anhalt have also voted for AfD politician Hans-Thomas Tillschneider to be one of the deputy speakers in the chamber.
This follows Tobias Rausch of the right-wing populist AfD being voted into the speaker's role earlier on Tuesday.
Tillschneider received 44 votes in favor in Tuesday's session, while 38 parliamentarians opposed his appointment. Nobody abstained from the vote, which was by secret ballot. The AfD has 39 seats in the chamber.
Lawmakers decided to elect three deputy speakers in total, with elections for the others expected to follow later.
Tillschneider, aged 48, is the deputy chair of the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt parliamentary group. He's an AfD veteran, having joined the party in 2013 soon after it was founded.
Tillschneider is a member of the identitarian movement, and was a member of the two AfD fringe groups — the so-called Flügel (wing) and its "Patriotic Platform" — that have since been formally disbanded. He also had close ties to the Pegida and Legida groups that organized anti-migrant protests in eastern Germany.
As well as his strong views on Islam and migration, Tillschneider is also known for his ties to Vladimir Putin's Russia. He was one of three AfD parliamentarians to visit Russia in September 2022, barely six months after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine , in a visit that AfD party co-leader Alice Weidel rapidly disowned as a "private trip" and "not productive."
Since 2023, Tillschneider has written a monthly column for the Vedomosti newspaper in Russia. He attended the 73rd birthday celebrations for Putin at the Russian Embassy in Berlin last October.
The outgoing premier of Saxony-Anhalt says he can't explain where an additional four votes backing the AfD's Tobias Rausch as the state's new parliamentary speaker came from.
In a first for the far-right party, 35-year-old Rausch was elected to the post on Tuesday with the help of the populist BSW party (see entry below).
The Christian Democratic Union (CDU) parliamentary group leadership had recommended that its 15 lawmakers in the state parliament abstain from voting.
But CDU regional leader and current state Premier Sven Schulze said it had become clear by this morning that not all the party's lawmakers planned to do so.
Some indicated that they planned to vote "no," Schulze said in comments to the German press agency DPA. "But none of us said we would vote 'yes,'" he added. "Not a single one."
Rausch was elected with 48 votes in favor and 29 against from 82 eligible votes in the secret ballot. There were five abstentions.
The AfD holds 39 seats in the parliament and the BSW five, meaning Rausch also got backing from members of other parties besides the AfD and BSW.
The center-left Social Democrats demanded answers, with the party's general secretary, Tim Klüssendorf, calling for the CDU to "immediately clarify who from within its ranks may have considered this disastrous decision to be right."
Klüssendorf also criticized the BSW for supporting Rausch's election.
"The BSW has made a conscious decision to elect, for the first time since 1945, a politician from a far-right party to the leadership of a German parliament," Klüssendorf told the Rheinische Post newspaper.
In addition to the CDU, the Social Democrats and the BSW, the Left party and the Greens are also represented in the state's parliament. Except for the BSW, the other parties have refused to work with the AfD, but some combination of them cast a secret vote for Rausch.
The Volksbank Köln Bonn in western Germany has agreed to part ways with a board member, Jürgen Neutgens, after a scandal over a loan he authorized to Cologne 's large brothel, Pascha.
It made the announcement on Tuesday, several months after placing Neutgens on leave and commissioning an independent law firm to investigate the transaction for potential wrongdoing.
"The investigation ... found no indications of financial irregularities or actions contravening obligations in the loan processes or the business relationship," the bank said in a press release . "Nevertheless the past weeks have weighed considerably on everyone involved."
Against this backdrop, the bank said the parties involved had mutually concluded that "a trusting and candid cooperation for the future can no longer be continued on the appropriate foundation."
It said both sides had agreed to confidentiality on the further details and terms, and thanked Neutgens for his service and wished him well for the future.
The loan was issued amid the restrictions of the COVID pandemic, which took a severe toll on the sex industry in Germany and led to the Pascha brothel in Cologne filing for insolvency and then changing ownership .
A family from China, or more specifically the autonomous casino-rich region of Macao, bought the business. But they needed a bridging loan of around €5 million (roughly $5.6 million at today's exchange rates) to cover part of the purchase price when their funds were held up in Hong Kong.
A typical German Christmas speciality intended as a gift for Pope Leo XIV was driven to Rome in an official vehicle from the state of Saxony after it was deemed unsuitable for air transport, officials revealed on Tuesday.
The 4-kilogram (8.8-pound) cake, a so-called stollen, which was made in the Ore Mountains in eastern Germany, was taken by Saxon Premier Michael Kretschmer to the Vatican for a private audience at the end of September.
The cake was reportedly too large to be taken into the cabin and too fragile to be placed in the aircraft hold, the officials said.
No information was provided on the cost by the officials at the Saxon State Chancellery.
The vehicle also transported other presents and documents.
The leader of the Green parliamentary party in Saxony-Anhalt , Susan Sziborra-Seidlitz, has vowed to defend democracy following the election of a member of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) , Tobias Rausch, as parliamentary speaker.
The election of the member of a confirmed right-wing extremist, anti-constitutional party as house speaker meant that a "border" had been crossed, she said.
"We will not allow ourselves to be intimidated, and we will not sit by when rights here or those of the people in this state are to be curtailed," she added.
Earlier in her address, she said that if the AfD were to take power in the state, her party would "speak out if people were denigrated because of their origins, beliefs or lifestyle."
Sziborra-Seidlitz said Saxony-Anhalt could not afford for "exclusion to become the political brand of this parliament and our state."
The AfD emerged from September elections as the strongest single force in parliament but has so far failed to find parties willing to enter into a coalition with it.

articles.title_orig: The world has nearly burned through its oil stockpile buffer, executives say
articles.title_zh: The world has nearly burned through its oil stockpile buffer, executives say
articles.content_orig:
LONDON, Oct 6 – The amount of oil in storage that is accessible to the global market is running low, industry executives said at a forum in London this week, making the market more fragile and putting upward pressure on prices.
Governments and energy companies have drawn oil from stockpiles to alleviate pressure in a global oil market facing unprecedented supply disruptions this year due to the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine .
“Less than six billion barrels of commercial inventories remain today, with the vast majority not practically available, so the system is already straining,” Amin Nasser, CEO of Saudi Arabia’s state oil company Saudi Aramco, said at the Energy Intelligence Forum in London.
More than one billion barrels of oil have been released mainly from onshore commercial inventories since the start of this year’s Middle East crisis , which was the last major tool in the box, Nasser said.
The International Energy Agency, the West’s oil watchdog and coordinator of its strategic oil reserves, is preparing to release 100 million barrels of crude and diesel to help alleviate soaring diesel prices, but it is not clear if some of that total will include volumes from its record first 400 million barrel release in March that hadn’t hit the market yet.
“It took a lot of negotiations, but it is 100 million,” Nasser said of the IEA decision. “Inventories are reaching a stress level. Only 10% or less is available, that’s why they struggle with 100 million barrels.”
World oil demand is about 102 million barrels per day, according to the IEA.
The loss of the oil market’s buffers has made the market more fragile, Chevron CEO Mike Wirth said on Tuesday, adding that this has increased oil’s price floor .
Oil market turmoil will continue beyond next year, executives said at the conference on Monday, as it could take years to refill inventories on top of meeting global demand.
Not all oil in storage is immediately usable because of operational factors like tank bottoms or oil sat in pipelines, as well as political factors like government rules dictating minimum levels of emergency stocks.
There is huge demand to build additional inventories around the globe, Nasser added. Kuwait Petroleum Corporation CEO Shaikh Nawaf Al-Sabah said his company is aiming to build out storage domestically and at its overseas refineries.
The world is reliant on the seaborne oil exports escaping the Middle East “to keep things in balance as we go through winter, because there aren’t any more inventories to drain in the West,” the CEO of commodities trader Vitol Russell Hardy said.
Stocks of crude ​oil in ‌the US Strategic Petroleum ​Reserve ​are at their ​lowest since October 1982, ​according to ​data from the ‌Department ⁠of Energy.
Natural gas inventories are also depleted, making prices vulnerable to spikes. A bad winter could bring about a “bloodbath” in the gas market in the first quarter of 2027 if storage hits minimal levels, Petronas CEO Tengku Muhammad Taufik ​said.

articles.content_orig:
By Charity L. Cohen / 10/06/2026 Alumni , College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences
EAST GREENSBORO, N.C. (Oct. 6, 2026) – Forever a North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University Aggie and now a Hillman College Falcon, former Mister A&T Joshua Suiter ‘22 is starring in the Netflix reboot of the 1980s and 1990s hit sitcom “A Different World.”
The series, which debuted at No. 1 on Netflix in the U.S., has already been renewed for a second season. It builds on the cultural impact of the original series, which helped shape national perceptions of historically Black college and university (HBCU) life and inspired generations of students.
Following a new generation of students at the iconic fictional HBCU, Hillman College, the sequel explores the lives of today’s students while examining the legacy of those who came before them. The series’ writing team includes Ashley Laverne Jackson, daughter of late civil rights leader the Rev. Jesse Jackson ‘64.
Suiter portrays Andre, a fellow Hillman student alongside Deborah Wayne (Maleah Joi Moon), daughter of original characters Whitley (Jasmine Guy) and Dwayne (Kadeem Hardison). As Deborah begins her journey at Hillman, she works to establish her own identity beyond her parents’ legacy while experiencing the highs and challenges of campus life.
“Seeing all the love for Andre really hit home,” Suiter said. “He’s one of my favorite characters thus far, and we created him from scratch, so to know that the hard work is being received and folks want more encourages me to keep going.”
Suiter discovered his calling for acting and musical theater at 7, quickly realizing that hours spent studying lines and practicing techniques felt like minutes. That passion led him to N.C. A&T, where he earned a B.F.A. in professional theatre from the College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences.
While at A&T, Suiter built a strong foundation in the performing arts, gaining experience both on stage and behind the scenes. One of his notable performances was in “Ain’t Misbehavin’” during the university’s first Town & Gown Gala in 2019, where he first met Guy, who reprises her role as Whitley in the reboot.
In addition to acting, Suiter worked as a theater technician and developed skills in the marketing and business aspects of performance and the entertainment industry. This versatility helped propel him into his professional career.
“I came in as a creative, but what A&T did between Alpha Phi Alpha, the classes, talking business with professors and serving as Mister A&T sharpened me on the business side,” said Suiter. “It sharpened my networking skills while showing me how to be authentic to who I am.”
As a talented and emerging actor who most recently appeared in the Hulu series “All’s Fair,” performing alongside prominent Hollywood actors, starring in “A Different World” represents a full-circle moment for Suiter as an HBCU alumnus, bringing him into a reimagined version of a series he grew up watching.
“When you talk about an HBCU experience, I’m putting mine up there with the best of them,” he said. “I have so many experiences to pull from with the run of this show, with the character Andre. Hillman even has a heartbeat of its own, so it’s been fun exploring what that feels like as a student there, while still carrying that Aggie Pride in my heart.”

Using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers are investigating turbulent planetary systems in which worlds violently collide. This investigation could shed light on the hypothetical collision between Earth and a Mars-sized planetary body called Theia , which is thought to have spilled matter around our planet that coalesced to forge the moon billions of years ago.
Young planetary systems are notoriously violent, featuring young stars surrounded by disks of gas and dust called protoplanetary disks. Within these disks, small bodies called planetesimals collide and stick together to begin the process of forming planets. However, NASA's now-retired Spitzer Space Telescope discovered that there is a class of protoplanetary disks that are even more violent than usual, so-called extreme debris disks. These systems contain unusually large amounts of warm dust close to the young star, in the region similar to that occupied by rocky planets in the solar system.
Investigating extreme debris disks is challenging, partially because they are so rare. Scientists estimate that such systems exist around just 1% of stars. It is suspected that our sun was one of these rare stars.
A team of scientists set about investigating 21 extreme debris disks with the incredible observing power of the JWST . This included follow-ups on four of the five of these environments from Spitzer's archival data and 16 from the JWST, with 12 newly observed disks
"This is the first time we have gathered enough systems to truly understand this subclass that we call extreme debris disks," team leader Kate Su of the Space Science Institute in Boulder, Colorado, said in a statement . "Before the JWST, we had limited information. We knew that they are weird and very different from the typical cold debris disks that we know, like Vega and Fomalhaut .
"Now that we have more data, we can pin down what these disks represent for planet formation and evolution."
The researchers discovered that there are three properties common to extreme debris disks. They contain smaller dust grains than those found in "classic" protoplanetary disks, a high concentration of warm dust, and irregular variations in brightness.
The next step was to discover what was driving these features. To do this, the team investigated the minerals that composed the disks they investigated, finding they could be categorized as silica-rich or silica-poor.
This told the scientists which type of collisions were occurring in those disks and producing impact debris. These collisions may also help account for its variability in brightness seen in these systems.
"To just see their mid-infrared emission and beautiful spectral features with the JWST, which allowed us to identify their compositions, was the most exciting thing for me," team member Agnes Kospal of Konkoly Observatory in Budapest, Hungary, said. "We have no other way to study these planetary embryos directly because they are too small."
The researchers think that silica-rich disks are produced by high-energy impacts of Mars-sized objects, in which most of the material is vaporized. Silica-poor disks are created by less energetic events from roughly moon-sized bodies grazing each other.
From their sample, around one-third of extreme debris disks are silica-rich disks. These were found only around stars younger than 300 million years. Silica-poor disks, on the other hand, were found around stars with a broad range of ages. They also often show greater brightness variability than silica-rich disks. The researchers propose that this variability in brightness is caused by the rapid evolution of fresh debris through further impacts and changes in the orbits of the system's occupants.
The findings can now be applied to the solar system to build a better picture of its 4.6-billion-year evolution. Simulations recreating the earliest era of the solar system show that terrestrial planets, such as Earth, should form within the first few hundred million years.
That lines up with the ages of observed silica-rich extreme debris disks and also aligns with the estimated formation of the Earth and the moon around 100 million years after the sun formed.
The solar system likely also went through a silica-poor extreme disk phase during a period called the Late Heavy Bombardment . It is during this period that scientists think collisions may have caused the solar system's gas giants to migrate from close to the sun to the positions they now occupy.
"How rocky planets formed and giant planets evolved are part of the broader story of the solar system’s formation. It’s all one story," said Su. "Our work on extreme debris disks helps us bring together the big picture of what we currently understand."
The team's research was published on Thursday (Oct. 1) in The Astrophysical Journal .
